I have also just recently found a stable job and have received my first tax return (yay!). I am soon to be 26, working a full time job and paying my small credit cards on time every month. My score has gone up since the beginning but I am still sitting at the low/mid 600s.

My question is, should I use my tax return and buy a beater car so that I am able to drive again (been about 2 years without a car, because I keep buying beaters) or should I just pay off both my credit cards and only use them sparingly so that my score goes up more and apply later for an auto loan?

[NA] What's the best way to raise my credit score and potentially apply for a car loan?

Keep your cards open. Average age of accounts matter.
Pay them down = lower utilization ratios = higher credit.
Check your credit report for any negative marks and get those corrected.

Do you have a budget? It will help assess transportation options.

I'm working on budgeting myself. I use Mint and check myself regularly by keeping a planner as well on when certain bills are due. I'd say 70% I am good and keep everything level. I am on time paying my bills and I try to do my grocery shopping once a month. But that money left over doesn't always go towards savings. As far as transportation I have been lucky to work with my roommate so we carpool everyday and when my boyfriend has time he takes me to the store. It feels like what little money I have to spend freely I have a difficult time putting away or buying "luxury" items (clothes, socializing, etc)

You're on the right track.

Most banks and credit unions will let you setup a sub-account for free. Try taking the leftover money in your budget and splitting it - part to the "fun money" sub account, and the rest to savings to buy a vehicle.

If you are in debt, and have no savings, and no credit, and you've already been getting to work for 2 years without a car, then you should do other things before buying a car.

Order of steps to follow:

1) Use your tax return to pay off your debts. Do NOT choose the option of going further into debt. Do not pass this step before going on to Step 2!

2) Save up an emergency fund in cash, that equals 3 to 6 months worth of your monthly expenses. Note: If you can't complete the bare minimum of Step 2, ownership of a car will probably ensure you remain broke and in debt.

3) Now that you completed step 2, you've proven you can walk the walk. Start saving money for a car, which you will buy in cash, the price of which will be capped at 10% - 15% of your annual salary. Putting a few grand down (NOT touching the E-fund!) and financing a few grand will leave you a very manageable payment. If you can, just hold out until you can pay 100% cash and you won't have to finance a thing. Think that "beater" car is too ugly? I'll bet not having a car payment will make it look a lot prettier.

Note on credit score: You won't reach the upper-echelons of credit scores without AGE on your credit accounts. There is no way around this. I recommend that young people get a credit card with a big-name bank (Wells Fargo, Chase, someone who is NOT going to go out of business) and maybe something like a Home Depot Card (you plan to have a house someday?) and plan to KEEP THEM FOREVER. If you already have one or two of those, just hang on to them. When your credit accounts hit 5, 10, 15 years of age in good standing, you will see your credit jump each time. People who jump in and out of store cards and close and cancel stupid cards for stupid reasons end up never having an "average age" of accounts more than 1-3 years, and then they wonder why their credit is 650 forever. Strive for 15-year accounts, that's 800+ credit territory. It doesn't even matter what the interest-rates and terms are on the cards. You should be making small purchases and paying them off immediately anyway.

For buying a car, try to buy something used, of course. Preferably from a senior citizen (yes an old lady car) from a make and model that is ranked highly by Edmunds as "lowest TCO (total cost of ownership)". Taxes, title fees, insurance, and repairs all have to be paid for. Most people go wrong in at least one of these categories. They buy "cool" cars that have poor reliability, or foreign cars that have expensive replacement parts, or 2-door sedans or SUVs that are expensive to insure. Also, find a car with small wheels, to save on tires. Tires for my old compact car? $400 for the whole car. Tires for a 1-ton pickup? $400 PER TIRE!
